speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock the hon. gentleman from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) was asking for an expression of opinion from the department in regard to making special arrangements for the surrender of an Indian reserve situated in the valley of the Fraser near the experimental farm at Agassiz, and close to the Canadian Pacific Railway line, and in what might be called the very heart of the best agricultural district in British Columbia. He was anxious to know if special arrangements might not be made in regard to the surrender of this reserve, Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
while awaiting a decision on the general question of dealing with reserves throughout the province. The Indian Department is very well aware of the conditions surrounding this particular reserve. One objection to making a special case of this reserve is that it is almost identical in circumstances with many other reserves throughout the province, and that so far from being a special case it is rather a specimen case. In the opinion of the department it is not desirable under such circumstances to make special arrangements in regard to a single case when that arrangement cannot be made applicable to all similar cases. The natural conditions in the province of British Columbia are such that in securing lands for the settlement of the Indian bands in that province and permitting them the right of selection, it has come about that in almost every valley, and adjoining almost every white settlement in every valley, and it might almost be said adjoining almost every point at which there is white settlement in every valley, there is an Indian reserve. This comes about by reason of the topographical conditions which naturally separated the Indians into small bands, each band being resident in a single valley or in a single part of a certain valley. And so, we have in the province of British Columbia, 1,000 Indian reserves scattered about through the valleys and naturally quite as numerous in the parts of the province that are occupied by white settlers as in the parts which are not. This question of the Indian reserves in British Columbia is of paramount importance in the development of that province. It will be understood that in a country so mountainous as British Columbia the valleys have special value, and so it is that where these reserves are situated, at the present time (within the last few years particularly under the development that has taken place) these lands have become of extra special value, so that while there was a question arising about the location of these reserves a few years ago that question has now become a burning one and I might say a dominant question in the development of the province. It may seem strange that such a small area should be so very important in a province with such a stupendous total area, but when you take that area and split it up into a thousand parcels and place each of these parcels in a locality which has been selected by those who knew the province best, you have certainly a very serious bar to the settlement and development of that province. The tenure of Indian lands in British Columbia is somewhat different from that prevailing in other parts of Canada. In all other parts of Canada the Indian is held to be the absolute owner of the land; he is the absolute proprietor not as an individual but as a community. In British Columbia, however, that

is not the position as it has been understood. I need not go into any lengthy explanation at the moment, but in the ease of Indian reserves in British Columbia until the administration of this government, up to a certain point it was understood that while the Indian owned the land he occupied, and while that land was administered by the Dominion government as the guardian and trustee of the Indian, the government of the province had what was called a reversionary interest in all those Indian reserves.
The Indian Department recognized this as being the position; and so, in any disposition that was attempted to be made of Indian lands for the benefit of the Indians, the reversionary interest of the province of British Columbia was always considered. What the value of that reversionary interest might be was not a matter that could very well be settled; but it was always recognized and kept in view in any transactions in Indian lands. Therefore, Indian lands in British Columbia had not the same value to the Indians that they would have had had they been held under the same tenure as lands in the northwest provinces or in Ontario. But it was always considered that the interest of the Indians was paramount to that of the province. Now, recognizing the desirability of bringing those lands which were not in use by the Indians into profitable occupation, and at the same time securing for the Indians the full benefit of their interest in them, which is in accordance with the principle of administration of Indian lands observed by the Canadian government ever since it undertook to handle Indian lands-when an application was made by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for a certain part of the Metla-katla reserve for the purpose of a terminus for the railroad on the Pacific coast, the Indian Department approached the Indians occupying the reserve, and negotiated a surrender of their rights in some 13,000 acres of the reserve, for which the Grand Trunk Pacific Company paid something like $100, 000, which is at the credit of the Metla-katla Indian band. In the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, it was especially stipulated under seal that the reversionary interest of the province of British Columbia was not in any way prejudiced by this transfer of Indian rights. The Indian Department, I may say, believed that the transaction was in the interest of the Indians, in the interest of the province, and in the interest of all Canada, as well as in the interest of the railway company; and believed that to such a degree that before entering into the arrangement with the railway company, the Dominion government asked the province to waive its reversionary interest in those lands, believing that the province would
benefit sufficiently by the proposed transaction to warrant it in doing so. The provincial government, however, in their wisdom declined to waive the reversionary interest, and so the sale was made subject to that reversionary interest. A little later certain communications passed between the government of the province and the government of the Dominion in regard to this particular transaction, and in regard to the general question of dealing with these Indian reserves, with a view of getting the question into such a position as would enable the Indian Department to dispose of unused or unneeded Indian lands for the benefit of the Indians, and for the benefit of the settlement of the province. In the course of the correspondence, the government of British Columbia saw fit to take a position which had not previously been contemplated-a position different from that which it formerly held, as we understood it; and in an order in council dated the 28th of February, 1907, the provincial government states its position in these words:
It follows, then, that the Dominion government has no right or power to make or grant a lease or transfer of any Indian reserve, or portion of a reserve, in this province, and that where any lease or transfer has been made, the reserve or portion of a reserve so leased or transferred now belongs absolutely to the province. It would appear that in at least three instances transfers or leases have been made by the Dominion government of portions of Indian reserves, namely 3'21 acres of the Myuke reserve in Kootenay, 7 acres of the False Creek reserve1 in Vancouver, and 13 -567 acres of the Port Simpson reserve. These lands now belong to and should be claimed by the province.
That is to say, the provincial government, instead of claiming a reversionary interest, claimed an absolutely proprietary interest in the lands, declaring that the Indians were merely the occupants, and not in any sense the owners of the lands. It must be evident that this declaration on the part of the province absolutely prohibited the Dominion government from taking any further action in regard to the alienation of Indian lands. The Dominion government could not undertake to dispossess the Indians without securing value to^ them for their interest, whatever it might be. I presume that the committee will recognize that as being the correct position. It is the traditional position of the British government in Canada, and has been the unaltered position of the Canadian government ever since it has been handling Indian affairs. Therefore the Indian Department, in undertaking to deal with Indian lands in the province of British Columbia, could only be a party to their alienation when assured that the Indians were receiving full value for what-

ever interest they had in the lands. It must be evident that unless a title can be given for the land, no man will pay his money for it. The position therefore is this:
A cloud is placed on the title to Indian land by the government of the province of British Columbia which prevents any one from investing his money in it, and thus causes a tie-up in the situation unless the Dominion government is prepared to take, the ground that the Indian has no right in these lands.
Where the Indians abandon their reserve, as they did around Kaien Island, and the reversionary right brings that back to the Crown, you could not interfere with the title then.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Indians did not abandon their reserve, but sold a part and retained the remainder.

As long as the Indians were settled on that land and the tribe remained, it was theirs, but if they vacated it and went away, it reverted to the Crown; and the contention was that the band abandoned their reserve and went to the United States. Afterwards, however, a portion of another band came and squatted on this reserve and took possession of it, but the province, under the reversionary right, owned the land and pretended that the others were only squatters.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The province did- not make any pretention with regard to abandonment, but simply claimed that if the Indians either sold the land or ceased to occupy any portion of the reserve, it became vested in the province. I am not arguing the question of the validity of that contention, but I am saying that such a declaration by the British Columbia government necessarily tied up the land and prevented this government disposing of it and at the same time discharging its trust to the Indians. That being the case, and we did not in any way wish to take any action which would bring us into conflict with the province, but still, not considering that we would be warranted in acceding to their position, we stated that we would be willing to facilitate a decision by a court of competent jurisdiction. It seemed to us that by reference to the proper court, we would obtain a decision either acknowledging the rights of the Indians or stating that they had no rights, and in the latter case relieve the Indian Department of all responsibility in the matter. We have not since been able to come to an arrangement with the province for the submission of the matter to the decision of the courts, and consequently the land is absolutely tied up, and the Indian Department is prevented from dealing with it with the view of releasing such portion to Mr. OLIVER,
settlement as is not needed by the Indians, and giving the Indians the benefit of whatever legal rights they have in the property. The fact that an arrangement has not yet been come to is not due to any laxity on the part of this government. On September 24, 1906, the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs wrote the premier of British Columbia making a certain suggestion as to the settlement of the dispute. On December 5, 1906, no answer having up to that date been received, another letter was sent asking a reply, and on March 13, 1907, the following reply was received by the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs:
Adverting to your letter of Dec. 5, 1906 and other correspondence with reference to the Indian reserve question in this province, I bee to state that the action of the federal government in connection with the Indian reserve in British Columbia has been so unsatisfactory of late that this government does not intend to enter into any further arrangement with the Dominion authorities.
Yours truly,
WiM. McBRIDE.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext: Roughly speaking an upset price is placed upon the lands. That is, the Indians agree to surrender the land for sale provided the land is not sold at a less figure than that agreed on, which of course varies in different reserves. On signing the surrender an arbitrary sum of so much per head is paid down to bind the bargain. Then a certain percentage of the total price received, varying from 20 per cent up to 50 per cent, is paidl to the Indians as it is received. That is for every dollar that is paid in on the purchase price of the land 50 cents may be paid direct to the Indians. From that 50 cents of course, is deducted the first payment made to bind the bargain. The balance, 50 cents, is funded and the interest on that is paid to the Indians each year, generally speaking at the same time as the treaty payments, an equal amount per head.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext:
The Indian items now being passed, I wish to say that on Friday last a number of questions were asked me and I promised to bring down the answers. Some of the gentlemen who asked the questions are not here, but I have the answers ready. First, I have an answer to the question of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche). The item for a bull shown in the Auditor's Report as being purchased for the Birtle agency from ' R. Logan, agent ' has not been detailed properly. It was, together with others, purchased at the Brandon sale of bulls out of funds advanced for the purpose, and Mr. Logan, who is the agent at Portage la Prairie, accounted for the money advanced. Nine bulls were bought at this sale; three for the Birtle agency (one charged to cattle vote and twe to bull fund) from the Cattle Breeders' Association, whose receipt is held by the Auditor General, at a cost of $261.20, delivered at Birtle, including transportation and other charges, and six for Portage la Prairie agency for $619.40, including transportation.
Then the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) asked a question about the payment of $16 to Dr. F. A. Rand, medical

officer for the Indians of Cumberland county, N.S. This was due to an outbreak of small-pox amongst the Indians. The payment was for special services rendered by the doctor in vaccinating the Indians at the different places where they are located in the county, viz.:
1907, Jan. 7. To visit to Halfway River
10 miles to vaccinate Indians	 $5 00
1907. Jan. 7. To vaccinate fourteen Indians at 25 cents each	 3 50
1907, Jan. 11. To visit to Springhill Junction to vaccinate Indians (25 miles) and vaccinating four at 25c..	3 50
1907, Jan. 30. To visit to Southampton
to vaccinate Indians (20 miles) and vaccinating nine at 25c	 4 00

speechtext: That reply simply means that it is not the duty of the officer to attend small-pox cases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext: Where they are not on the reserve. I understand these Indians were scattered about. There is, of course, a difference between small-pox and an ordinary disease. This is a special allowance for vaccination, but it is not the treatment of disease.

subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS

speechtext: In connection with the Chippewa Indians of Rama township in my constituency, there is an item of $250 to Dr. McLean, 12 months; another item, hospital attendance, Dr. McLean, $61, in I-84.

subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext: Dr. McLean gets $300 a year, $250 from the appropriation and $50 from the funds of the band. The special claim mentioned there is, I think, a hill for attendance on some Indian who was not a member of the band.

speechtext: Then there is another item: Medical attendance, Dr. A. P. Ardagh, $25; Dr. W. A. Henderson, $47.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext:
I assume those are for medical attendance on Indians who are nor members of the band, but who have come into the district and require medical attend ance. Then I have another answer to a question of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche). In regard to the payment of $200.50 to H. B. Rush, over and above the contract price for the erection of buildings at Kinistino reserve, the facts are that the department called for tenders in July, 1906. and Mr. Rush's tender was the lowest received. The contract, however, was not awarded at that time as a question had arisen as to whether it would not be advisable to erect the buildings at Nut Lake reserve instead of Kinistino, and this question was not decided until too late to build that year. The following spring, on March 15, 1907, Mr. Rush: was notified to proceed with the work and almost at once, on May 4, he drew the attention of the inspector to the fact that prices had increased and that he would like to he allowed the difference. Upon completion of the work, he put in a claim of $200.50 to cover the difference between the advance in the cost of materials between the date of his tender in 1906 and when he was notified to proceed with the work. The matter was referred to Mr. Inspector Chisholm for his report (copy of which is attached hereto) and payment was made upon his recommendation, as it was considered the contractor had a just claim, according to the facts and figures submitted.
The Auditor General made some inquiries in regard to this payment and the facts were placed before him. The tenders were as follows:	A. N. Claggett, $3,780; W.
Wortley, $3,575; H. B. Rush, $2,600.
Then, a question was asked with regard to the notice given to the lessees of a timber limit that their license would be terminated.

subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext: That is the question of the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr Smyth).

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext: Yes. The Indians of ths Spanish river reserve petitioned the department in November, 1907, to terminate the license as the licensees had held it over twenty-one years,, that they were only cutting small quantities annually, that it is contrary to agreement to hold the limit indefinitely and allow timber to become merchantable which was not merchantable when the license issued, but has since grown to be merchantable, that no bonus was paid for such and it never was surrendered for sale, that the licensees do not employ Indians and only work the limit with one contractor, and they have had ample time to remove the timber. The matter was referred to the Department of Justice, which replied that the surrender of the timber by the Indians only included timber that was merchantable at the time and not what became merchantable since; that the license is confined to timber then licensed and the licensees may be required to remove what remains of the timber covered by the license within a reasonable time at the end of which the license will be determined. The licensees were advised accordingly, on November 24, 1908, and notified that as ample time had been given for the removal of the timber actually covered by their license, the department is obliged to terminate it on April 30 next.

speechtext: Have the Indians of Manitoulin island the right to_ lease land for the purpose of boring for oil?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS
speechtext:
They are the absolute owners of the reserve and of the minerals and natural resources as well. Therefore, I think there can be no question that they have the right to lease. Of course, the Indian Department, as their guardians, negotiates the lease so that any lease that is made is subject to the consideration and approval of the department. The Indian Department is responsible for the lease being in due form and provident.
